claims.text: A narrow distribution of exchange interactions is the primary mechanism governing a strong low-field magnetocaloric response in rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys.
FCC-metal additive incorporation combined with heat treatment can reduce the distribution of exchange energies.
The untreated NiFeCoCr-based baseline has a broader distribution of exchange interactions than an additive-containing, heat-treated alloy.
Optimized elemental distribution produces a more homogeneous local exchange environment.
Reduced lattice distortion contributes to local exchange-interaction homogeneity.
Exchange-interaction homogeneity minimizes the spread in local Curie temperatures.
A narrower distribution of exchange energies leads to a sharper, more abrupt second-order magnetic phase transition.
A sharper second-order transition produces a larger magnetic entropy change per unit applied field.
Exchange homogeneity reduces magnetic pinning and consequently lowers hysteresis losses.
The intervention will maintain the alloy's mechanical robustness.
The intervention will maintain or improve rapid heat transfer.
Cu or Ag can substitute for Pd as a lower-cost FCC-metal additive and may provide similar tunability because the additive role is predominantly structural.
NiFeCoCrPdx alloys exhibit a second-order magnetic transition whose critical temperature can be tuned from approximately 100 K to above room temperature.
The proposed mechanism should apply near room temperature and at applied fields of 1 T or less.
The mechanism should be limited to rare-earth-free HEAs with similar compositions and primarily FCC structures.
Relative to the untreated baseline, the treated alloy should exhibit a higher peak magnetic entropy change at low fields.
Relative to the baseline, the treated alloy should exhibit a sharper but continuous magnetic transition and reduced magnetic hysteresis.
Magnetic-refrigeration materials require large magnetic entropy change as well as adequate heat transfer, conductivity, chemical and mechanical stability, and low hysteresis losses.
